sources.title: Igor Stravinsky (Q7314) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-15): English label 'Igor Stravinsky', description 'Russian, French, and American composer (1882-1971)', Korean label present, instance of human, born 1882 (the entity carries several date values covering the Julian and Gregorian dates), died 6 April 1971 in New York City, citizenship values including the Russian Empire, Russia, France and the United States. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Library of Congress Music Division research guide, 'Igor Stravinsky: A Guide to Primary and Secondary Resources at the Library of Congress' (author Paul Allen Sommerfeld, Music Reference Specialist; Introduction and Music Manuscripts pages, last updated July 2026) -- CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE (with the Boosey & Hawkes biography): the national library's own statement that Stravinsky is 'one of the most influential composers of the 20th century', and its description of its holdings: over 40 music manuscripts in his hand (among them a manuscript of the ballet Apollon musagete commissioned by the Elizabeth Sprague Coolidge Foundation, Agon, Mavra, Oedipus Rex and the Symphony in C) and, in the Igor Stravinsky / Robert Craft collection, publisher's proofs carrying his holograph corrections, including early proofs of Threni with 'corrections and instructions to the engravers and the publisher' and numerous corrected copies of Requiem Canticles, Variations, Movements and Canticum Sacrum. Institutional description of archival objects, neutral in tone. Read in full (the Special Collections, Published Music, Music Literature, Iconography, Lectures and Databases tabs were not opened).

Boosey & Hawkes, 'Igor Stravinsky' composer page (Snapshot summary and Biography tab, the publisher's own biography reproduced with its permission note) -- CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE (with the Library of Congress guide): his publisher's account of the career arc (study with Rimsky-Korsakov, The Firebird for Diaghilev's Ballets russes in 1910 bringing 'sudden international prominence', Petrushka and The Rite of Spring as 'one of the major landmarks in the history of music' that 'marked the coming of modernism in music' and met 'astonishment and hostility', the smaller-scale theatrical ventures such as The Soldier's Tale with Ramuz prompted by economic conditions, Pulcinella launching the neoclassical phase that ran from the 1920s to the 1940s through Oedipus Rex, Symphony of Psalms and The Rake's Progress, the ballets generally made with George Balanchine, and the 1957 ballet Agon as 'one of the most unexpected stylistic volte-faces in modern music' after he began studying Webern intensely in 1952), with his work as a pianist and then conductor of his own music and the near-complete recorded legacy. Publisher's promotional page, admiring in tone: its sentence that he is 'widely regarded as the most original and influential composer of the 20th century' is the publisher's own claim and is not repeated as fact in any row or card. Read in full except the work list, timeline, news and discography tabs.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Igor Stravinsky' (article by Eric Walter White, fact-checked by Britannica's editors, last updated 11 September 2026; the page's AI-generated summaries were not used) -- encyclopaedia biography: a Russian-born composer 'whose work had a revolutionary impact on musical thought and sensibility just before and after World War I' and 'whose compositions remained a touchstone of modernism for much of his long working life'; the Diaghilev ballets (The Firebird, 25 June 1910, 'a dazzling success'; Petrushka, 1911; The Rite of Spring, 29 May 1913, 'an early modernist landmark' whose premiere 'provoked one of the more famous first-night riots in the history of musical theatre'); the wartime small-scale works including The Soldier's Tale (1918); the Neoclassical idiom of the 1920s to the 1950s (Octet, Oedipus Rex, Symphony of Psalms, Symphony in C, Symphony in Three Movements, The Rake's Progress, 'his only full-length opera'); the 1950s serial works (Cantata, Septet, Agon, Canticum Sacrum, Threni, Requiem Canticles, 1966); the Royal Philharmonic Society Gold Medal (1954) and Wihuri Sibelius Prize (1963). It also states that his 1936 autobiography and his six later collaborations with Robert Craft are 'factually unreliable'. Encyclopaedic, neutral in tone. Read in full.

Library of Congress Music Division blog 'In the Muse', 'Acquisition Highlights for the Past Year: A Top Five List' (December 2023), item 2, 'Two Groups of Igor Stravinsky Correspondence' -- curators' note: Stravinsky as 'by any reckoning, one of the most important and influential classical composers of the twentieth century', the Library as 'the major American repository for original scores and correspondence of Stravinsky' (earliest music manuscript the Apollon-Musagete score, performed in 1928 in the Library's Coolidge Auditorium, then about 50 more manuscripts), and two new groups of letters, including 72 items of 1941-47 correspondence with the Associated Music Publishers editor Arthur Mendel that 'center on pre-publication changes to several of Stravinsky's works'. Institutional, admiring but factual. Read the Stravinsky item only.

Poppy Farr (Music Manuscripts and Archives Cataloguer), 'The life and music of Stravinsky in two newly catalogued collections', British Library blog, 3 June 2026 -- archive cataloguer's account of the Boosey & Hawkes production materials (Stravinsky the best represented composer, over 60 files): his signing with Boosey & Hawkes in the 1940s, his revising of 'many of his compositions' and producing new editions in the decades that followed (citing Helen Wallace's history of the publisher), the 1956 Mavra vocal score with his handwritten revisions of 1966 and several proof copies showing 'the repeated revisions the score underwent' before the 1968 edition, a score of Elegy for J.F.K. with his amendments to dynamics, articulation and phrasing, and the printed score he used to conduct the 1948 premiere of Orpheus. The Dartington Summer School visit (accommodation, catering and other hospitality details) is private and was not used. Archival description, neutral in tone. Read in full.

Arnold Schönberg Center, Vienna, 'Three satires for mixed chorus op. 28' (composition page with the program note by Agnes Grond) -- the Schoenberg archive's own note on the 1925/26 choral satires: Schoenberg's explanation in a letter that he wrote them 'when I was very much angered by attacks of some of my younger contemporaries', his four targets named in the foreword (those who seek salvation 'in the middle of the road', those who look backwards, 'folklorists' and 'all the ...ists' he sees as 'mannerists'), and the note's statement that in the third satire, 'Der neue Klassizismus', apart from the musicologist Hugo Riemann 'Stravinsky was the main target'. Institutional note from the rival camp's archive, adversarial in tone towards Stravinsky's neoclassicism and concerned with his music, not his conduct. Read in full.

Jacques Amblard, 'Survey of works by Igor Stravinsky' (translated by Peter Asimov), IRCAM-Centre Pompidou B.R.A.H.M.S. composer database, updated 2015 -- scholarly overview essay: the Rite of Spring as 'a canonical milestone of music history' and its repeated chord and ostinato as 'one of the most influential, even foundational, tools of twentieth-century music'; Schoenberg's 'der kleine Modernsky' in the Three Satires; the wartime reduction of forces (Soldier's Tale, Renard, Les Noces); Pulcinella and the neoclassical works; the later jazz-band pieces; the turn to serialism on the advice of Robert Craft; Adorno's judgement that neoclassicism was 'restoration' and Boulez's rejection of it; and Valerie Dufour's finding that he was 'a strategist' whose press appearances and interviews systematically preceded his concerts. Passages on politics, religion, psychoanalytic and mental-health speculation, and one 1941 anthem-arrangement episode were not used. Scholarly essay by an institutional research body, critical and admiring by turns. Read in full.

Jennifer Homans, 'Geniuses Together' (review of Charles M. Joseph, Stravinsky and Balanchine: A Journey of Invention, Yale University Press, 2002), The New York Review of Books, 19 December 2002 -- dance historian's review: the anecdote of Stravinsky answering 'Don't say about, there is no such thing as about' when Balanchine gave an approximate length for a dance, his insistence that music be 'transmitted' and not 'interpreted', the two men 'often seen bent over a score', Balanchine's deference to him, Stravinsky's extensive markings in his copy of de Lauze's Apologie de la danse (with Mersenne's notes) while composing Agon and his use of Bach's Concerto for Two Violins in his own Violin Concerto, Balanchine's account of the Apollon musagete score as a revelation; the review's own view that Joseph is good on the music and weak on the dances. Passages on his political and religious outlook were not used. Independent critic's review of a scholarly study (the one scholarly perspective is Joseph's, so this review and the Brooklyn Rail review of the same book are one source of facts, not two). Read in full.

Paul Grimstad, review of Charles Joseph, Stravinsky & Balanchine: A Journey of Invention (Yale University Press, 2002), The Brooklyn Rail, October 2002 -- composer-critic's review of the same scholarly study: Stravinsky's 'occasionally tyrannical exactitude in matters of metronomic execution' at the first Chant du rossignol rehearsals (a pianola cranked by an 'autocratic' composer), Stravinsky's falling out with Diaghilev 'for business reasons', his own description of Apollo as his 'ballet blanc', the all-string Apollo score that resulted from a 'tangle of correspondence' with the Library of Congress about its auditorium, the origins of Agon in Webern's miniatures, Isaac's Choralis Constantinus, 17th-century French dance manuals and T. S. Eliot's verse, his switch to serialism as 'one of the last major compositional strongholds against the growing orthodoxy of serial technique' giving way, and the reviewer's criticisms of Joseph's method. Independent critic's review that counts, with the Homans review of the same book, as one scholarly perspective (Joseph's). Read in full.

Robert Craft, 'Stravinsky & Balanchine', The New York Review of Books, 8 October 1998 -- first-person account by Stravinsky's long-time associate, who says he was the only witness to the making of Agon and The Flood: how the two men's collaboration changed from the imperious handling of Balanchine over Jeu de cartes in 1937 to the joint plotting of Orpheus and the 'equal partner from conception to execution' of Agon, Balanchine persuading Stravinsky to expand the Orpheus pas de deux and to repeat the prelude of The Flood, and the order and titles of the Agon dances written down by Stravinsky as they talked. Insider account by one person with a stake in the story (Britannica calls his collaborative books factually unreliable), so used only as one perspective alongside the scholarly and critical sources, never alone. Passages on Balanchine's state of mind and religious feeling were not used. Read in full.

Ryan Wenzel, 'Modern Antiquity' (review of New York City Ballet's Stravinsky-Balanchine repertory season), The Brooklyn Rail, October 2012 -- dance critic's review: Balanchine choreographed 'at least 45 ballets' to Stravinsky's music; the Apollo-Orpheus-Agon 'Greek trilogy' as showing how 'both artists were always in the business of self-reinvention' (Stravinsky moving from the 17th-and-18th-century French style of Apollo to serial music in Agon); Balanchine's remark that the Apollo score 'in its discipline and restraint, in its sustained oneness of tone and feeling' was 'a revelation'; the success of Orpheus in 1948 that led to the New York City Ballet. Passages on the 2012 dancers were not used. Independent critic's review, admiring. Read in full.

Tom Vitale (NPR, Weekend Edition Saturday), 'Then The Curtain Opened: The Bracing Impact Of Stravinsky's Rite', 25 May 2013 (read as published by KUNC) -- public-radio feature for the centenary with the critic Alex Ross (the two adjacent chords 'slammed together', accents landing in unexpected places, 'The Rite felt completely different') and the dance historian Lynn Garafola (Nijinsky's choreography as 'a new kind of ballet'), reporting that within a year of the premiere the score was hailed as a masterpiece and that Nijinsky's choreography was abandoned after the first run; it also quotes Stravinsky's 1965 recollection of the premiere (self). Independent journalism with two expert voices, admiring. Read in full.

James S. Murphy, 'Spring Fever', The Paris Review (On Music), 11 July 2013 -- essay by a musicologically trained writer on how the Rite premiere is remembered: scholars 'have called into question the size, the ferocity, and the immediate effects' of what was 'definitely a disturbance', Stravinsky leaving his seat 'only to watch backstage' and taking four or five curtain calls, Nijinsky counting time to the dancers all week, the London premiere and later Paris performances passing without major incident, and Diaghilev as a 'master marketer' who with Stravinsky made remarks to the press and invited critics to a preview so that the audience was 'primed'. Independent essay, skeptical of the riot legend and relaying Taruskin's argument at second hand. Read in full.

Katie Buzard, 'Did "The Rite of Spring" Really Incite a Riot?', Clef Notes, Illinois Public Media (WILL), 18 March 2025 -- public-media explainer drawing on contemporary reviews and on Taruskin and Gillian Moore: no evidence of physical altercations or of police being called, the earliest reports not using the word riot, the premiere preceded by press stories and open rehearsals, a score that took 17 orchestra rehearsals and over 130 dance calls, conductor Pierre Monteux's recollection of first hearing the piano reduction ('I was convinced he was raving mad'), Nijinsky's choreography described by Taruskin as 'ugly earthbound lurching and stomping', and the premiere's role in making the work an icon of modernism. Popular but well-referenced; used for the premiere context and counter-evidence on the riot, not for any trait row on its own. Read in full.

Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, item record 2014712545, 'Stravinsky' (Bain News Service, publisher; glass negative, [between ca. 1920 and ca. 1925]; call number LC-B2- 5464-2 [P&P]; reproduction number LC-DIG-ggbain-32392) -- checked for the portrait's rights: the record gives the Rights Advisory 'No known restrictions on publication' and the Bain collection's own statement reads 'There are no known copyright restrictions on the photographs in the George Grantham Bain Collection. Publicity rights may apply.' (credit line: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, with the reproduction number); the title is taken from the Bain negative and the summary identifies the sitter as the composer, pianist and conductor Igor Fyodorovich Stravinsky, the same photograph the Library's Stravinsky research guide uses as its illustration. The record was read through the Library's JSON interface and the rights statement through the Library's published rights data because the HTML pages returned HTTP 403 to direct download. Not used for any scoring.

Wikimedia Commons file page 'Stravinsky LCCN2014712545.jpg' -- checked for the portrait's file and licence: Bain News Service, publisher, from the Library of Congress (digital ID ggbain.32392), tagged with the Commons Bain and public-domain licence tags and the Library's 'No known restrictions on publication' statement; original JPEG 5405 x 7487 pixels (Commons' own date field reads 1900, which conflicts with the Library's [between ca. 1920 and ca. 1925] and was not used). Not used for any scoring.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_stravinsky_britannica, src_stravinsky_boosey, src_stravinsky_ircam, src_stravinsky_npr_rite, src_stravinsky_brooklynrail_joseph, src_stravinsky_schoenberg_center | 1913-1957 | encyclopaedia + publisher's biography + IRCAM scholarly survey + public-radio feature with a critic + critic's review + rival camp's archive] Britannica calls The Rite of Spring a 'highly original composition, with its shifting and audacious rhythms and its unresolved dissonances' and 'an early modernist landmark'; on NPR the critic Alex Ross explains the two adjacent chords 'slammed together', the accents that 'start landing in unexpected places' and says 'The Rite felt completely different'; IRCAM's Amblard credits the repeated polytonal chord and ostinato with giving rise to 'one of the most influential, even foundational, tools of twentieth-century music'; Boosey & Hawkes (his publisher, admiring) says the blend of melodic primitivism and rhythmic complexity 'marked the coming of modernism in music' and calls Agon (1957) 'one of the most unexpected stylistic volte-faces in modern music'; Grimstad says that in the serial Agon he kept 'his utterly unique sense of pulse and color' within a method that 'in other hands is often only about control'. Against this, IRCAM records Adorno's view that the long neoclassical period was 'restoration' and Boulez's rejection of it, and the Schoenberg archive's note names Stravinsky as the main target of the satire on the 'new classicism', so the originality of the middle period was contested by rival camps, which keeps the row below the top band. Several independent documented instances across the 1913 score and the 1950s serial turn, from encyclopaedic, scholarly, critical and adversarial sources, so documented at a moderate-high confidence. LEAD REVIEW CORRECTION (Roster50, before eligibility, downward only): the strongest rows rest on encyclopaedic and publisher assessments of the works and on archive holdings, with Robert Craft (one insider perspective) and the unreliable autobiography kept out; score and confidence lowered.

experimentation.rationale: [src_stravinsky_britannica, src_stravinsky_boosey, src_stravinsky_brooklynrail_nycb, src_stravinsky_brooklynrail_joseph, src_stravinsky_ircam | 1918-1966 | encyclopaedia + publisher's biography + critic's review of a repertory season + critic's review of a scholarly study + IRCAM scholarly survey] Britannica says The Soldier's Tale (1918) 'eclectically incorporates ragtime, tango, and other modern musical idioms', that after the war he 'abandoned the Russian features of his early style and instead adopted a Neoclassical idiom', and that in the 1950s 'a series of cautiously experimental works' (the Cantata, the Septet, In Memoriam Dylan Thomas) preceded Agon and Threni; Boosey & Hawkes adds that Pulcinella reworked Pergolesi 'into something completely personal' and that he 'had ignored Schoenbergian serialism' until he began to study Webern 'intensely' in 1952, calling Agon the first work in which he embraced it wholeheartedly (Britannica, by contrast, calls Agon and Canticum Sacrum 'only intermittently serial' and Threni the work that applies a strict twelve-tone method, so no first claim is made here); Wenzel writes that both Stravinsky and Balanchine 'were always in the business of self-reinvention'; Grimstad traces Agon to 'typically eclectic Stravinskian obsessions of the moment' (Webern's miniatures, Isaac's Choralis Constantinus, 17th-century French dance manuals, Eliot's verse); IRCAM lists humorous works for jazz band written in the United States in the 1930s and 1940s. Several independent descriptions of at least three distinct stylistic departures over five decades, so documented at a moderate-high confidence. IRCAM and Britannica (through Craft's account) say the serial turn followed Craft's advice, so the initiative was shared, and Adorno judged the neoclassical turn 'restoration', so the experiments were not all received as innovations. LEAD REVIEW CORRECTION (Roster50, before eligibility, downward only): the strongest rows rest on encyclopaedic and publisher assessments of the works and on archive holdings, with Robert Craft (one insider perspective) and the unreliable autobiography kept out; score and confidence lowered.

adaptability.rationale: [src_stravinsky_boosey, src_stravinsky_ircam, src_stravinsky_britannica, src_stravinsky_brooklynrail_joseph | 1914-1938 | publisher's biography + IRCAM scholarly survey + encyclopaedia + critic's review of a scholarly study] Boosey & Hawkes says economic conditions prompted smaller-scale theatrical ventures such as The Soldier's Tale with Ramuz; IRCAM says the 'wartime drought of available musicians' and 'ergonomic efficiency' led him to strip down his 'grand style' for chamber-scale forces; Britannica says the war disrupted the Ballets Russes so that he 'could no longer rely on that company as a regular outlet', and that, having lost his property in Russia, he 'was compelled to earn his living as a performer' and wrote many works of the 1920s and 1930s for his own use as concert pianist and conductor; Grimstad, summarising Joseph, says he reduced the Apollon musagete score for a Library of Congress hall that could not hold the planned piano and harp, 'ingeniously' reducing it to an all-string orchestra with a solo violin after a 'tangle of correspondence' with the Library's music division. Four distinct episodes of re-scoping his work to available forces or markets, each from a different source, but the Apollon detail rests on one reviewer and the 1920s-30s detail on one encyclopaedia, so documented at a moderate confidence. The 1950s serial turn is counted under experimentation, not here.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_stravinsky_loc_guide, src_stravinsky_bl_blog, src_stravinsky_loc_blog, src_stravinsky_nyrb_homans, src_stravinsky_brooklynrail_joseph | 1925-1966 | national-library research guide + national-library archive blog + national-library curators' blog + critic's review of a scholarly study + second critic's review] The Library of Congress guide says its Stravinsky / Robert Craft collection holds publisher's proofs with his holograph corrections, including early proofs of Threni with 'corrections and instructions to the engravers and the publisher' and 'numerous corrected copies' of Requiem Canticles, Variations, Movements and Canticum Sacrum, and a Library curator says his 1941-47 correspondence with a music-publisher's editor 'center[s] on pre-publication changes to several of Stravinsky's works'; the British Library's cataloguer describes his handwritten 1966 revisions to the 1956 vocal score of Mavra (a new edition followed in 1968) with several proof copies showing 'the repeated revisions the score underwent', and a score of Elegy for J.F.K. carrying his amendments to dynamics, articulation and phrasing; Homans relays Balanchine's account that when he said a dance would last 'about' two and a half minutes Stravinsky answered 'there is no such thing as about' and asked for the exact time, and says Stravinsky insisted his music be accurately 'transmitted' and not 'interpreted'; Grimstad, summarising Joseph, says he had 'a reputation for his occasionally tyrannical exactitude in matters of metronomic execution'. Two national archives and a curators' note plus two critics' accounts of one scholarly study describe corrections and exactness over four decades, so documented at a moderate-high confidence; the sources record the revisions but give no motive for them and none is inferred. LEAD REVIEW CORRECTION (Roster50, before eligibility, downward only): the strongest rows rest on encyclopaedic and publisher assessments of the works and on archive holdings, with Robert Craft (one insider perspective) and the unreliable autobiography kept out; score and confidence lowered.

perfectionism.rationale: [src_stravinsky_bl_blog, src_stravinsky_boosey, src_stravinsky_nyrb_homans, src_stravinsky_nyrb_craft, src_stravinsky_brooklynrail_joseph | 1925-1966 | national-library archive blog + publisher's biography + critic's review + insider's account + second critic's review] The British Library says that in the decades after he signed with Boosey & Hawkes in the 1940s he 'set about revising many of his compositions and producing new editions' (citing Helen Wallace's history of the publisher), and Boosey & Hawkes lists Petrushka and The Rite of Spring as 'rev. 1947'; the repeated proof revisions of Mavra point the same way; Homans, Grimstad (both summarising Joseph) and Craft agree he demanded exact execution, with Craft writing that in 1937 he 'obliged Balanchine to jettison part of his choreography for Jeu de cartes' and that 'by all accounts' he treated his young collaborator 'imperiously' then, and Grimstad, relaying Joseph's conjecture, picturing an 'autocratic' composer cranking a pianola and 'yell-counting' to the dancers at the first Chant du rossignol rehearsals. Two or more independent episodes of revision and exacting standards, but no source uses the word perfectionist, none says why he revised, and the costs fell on collaborators, so strong inference at a modest confidence with a dual-edged impact.

collaboration.rationale: [src_stravinsky_nyrb_craft, src_stravinsky_nyrb_homans, src_stravinsky_brooklynrail_joseph, src_stravinsky_brooklynrail_nycb, src_stravinsky_boosey, src_stravinsky_britannica | 1910-1962 | insider's account + critic's review of a scholarly study + second critic's review + critic's review of a repertory season + publisher's biography + encyclopaedia] Craft, who says he was the only witness to the making of Agon and The Flood, writes that for Orpheus (1948) the two men 'plotted the scenario and dance numbers' together before a note was composed, that Balanchine persuaded Stravinsky to expand the Orpheus pas de deux and later to repeat the prelude of The Flood, and that for Agon Balanchine was 'an equal partner from conception to execution', the order and titles of the dances being Balanchine's, written down by Stravinsky as they talked; Homans, summarising Joseph, says the two were 'often seen bent over a score' and that Balanchine 'revered Stravinsky and deferred to him willingly'; Wenzel says Balanchine choreographed 'at least 45 ballets' to his music; Boosey & Hawkes and Britannica list the Ballets Russes commissions, Ramuz for The Soldier's Tale and Auden and Kallman for The Rake's Progress. Against this, Craft and Grimstad describe an imperious, 'autocratic' manner early on (Jeu de cartes, 1937; Chant du rossignol, 1925) and Grimstad says he 'had himself fallen out with Diaghilev for business reasons', so the pattern is a directing partner who became more reciprocal over time. The Balanchine detail comes largely from one insider (Craft, whose collaborative books Britannica calls factually unreliable) and one scholarly study seen through two reviews, so documented at a moderate confidence.

curiosity.rationale: [src_stravinsky_nyrb_homans, src_stravinsky_brooklynrail_joseph, src_stravinsky_boosey, src_stravinsky_ircam | 1919-1957 | critic's review of a scholarly study + second critic's review + publisher's biography + IRCAM scholarly survey] Homans, summarising Joseph, says Lincoln Kirstein sent Stravinsky a modern edition of the 17th-century dance treatise Apologie de la danse by Francois de Lauze with scholarly notes and excerpts by Marin Mersenne, that Stravinsky 'marked his copy of the book extensively' and referred to de Lauze and Mersenne while composing Agon, and shows 'keen interest' in Baroque discussions of metre, rhythm and the origins of dances; Grimstad names the other sources of Agon as Webern's miniatures, Isaac's Choralis Constantinus and Eliot's verse; Boosey & Hawkes says that after ignoring serialism he began in 1952 'to study Webern's music intensely' and that for Pulcinella he 'went back to the music of Pergolesi'; IRCAM adds that he took up the serial method at Craft's suggestion, so the prompt was partly external. Several documented episodes of studying earlier or unfamiliar material before composing, but they cluster on Agon and on one scholar's study, so documented at a moderate confidence.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_stravinsky_brooklynrail_joseph, src_stravinsky_brooklynrail_nycb, src_stravinsky_ircam, src_stravinsky_boosey | 1928-1957 | critic's review + second critic's review + IRCAM scholarly survey + publisher's biography] Grimstad reports that Stravinsky called Apollo his 'ballet blanc', hearing the 'austere translucence' of its string orchestra as approximating white hues, with harmony that sounds in spots as if it could be played on the white keys alone (his own view, relayed by a critic); Balanchine, quoted by Wenzel, said of the Apollo score 'In its discipline and restraint, in its sustained oneness of tone and feeling, the score was a revelation'; IRCAM describes a deliberate preference for dry timbres and for winds and brass over strings (Cocteau's 'sentimental blackmail') and an overture to The Rake's Progress that uses strings only for its first and last chord; Boosey & Hawkes names 'rhythmic energy and orchestral virtuosity' as hallmarks in every period and says the serial music that resulted was 'entirely his own' with 'a formal elegance'. Four distinct sets of documented timbral and formal choices from different observers, but the sensitivity is inferred from choices in his own art form and partly from his own stated view, so strong inference at a modest confidence.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_stravinsky_britannica, src_stravinsky_boosey, src_stravinsky_brooklynrail_joseph, src_stravinsky_ircam, src_stravinsky_parisreview | 1913-1957 | encyclopaedia + publisher's biography + critic's review + IRCAM scholarly survey + essay on the premiere] Britannica describes the 1913 Rite as 'Stravinsky's creative and daring music' that drew cheers and protests; Boosey & Hawkes calls the 1957 Agon 'one of the most unexpected stylistic volte-faces in modern music' after he 'had ignored Schoenbergian serialism', and Grimstad says he had been 'one of the last major compositional strongholds against the growing orthodoxy of serial technique' before it; IRCAM says he 'knew full well that he would never manage to satisfy the most rigorous serialists'. Against a reading as reckless, the same sources describe the serial turn as staged (the Cantata, Septet and other 'cautiously experimental works' first, per Britannica) and taken on Craft's advice when neoclassicism 'could no longer pass for modern' (IRCAM), and Murphy says the 1913 premiere was primed for scandal by Diaghilev, 'a master marketer', so the risks look calculated and shared. Two documented episodes with a mixed picture, so strong inference at a modest confidence.

provenance.notes: PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE: Wikidata wbgetentities (2026-10-15) for Q7314 returned en label 'Igor Stravinsky', description 'Russian, French, and American composer (1882-1971)', ko label present, born 1882 (several date values covering the Julian and Gregorian dates; Britannica and Boosey & Hawkes give 5 June old style, 17 June new style), died 1971-04-06 in New York City; the lead's hint was correct.
